text: A doctor sets a stranger's broken leg and is tried as a conspirator for it. The stranger is John Wilkes Booth; Samuel A. Mudd is sentenced to life and shipped out to Shark Island. John Ford's interest in 1936 is less in the assassination than in what a country does with its rage once the man it wants is out of reach, and the answer here is procedural: a tribunal, a transfer, a wall, the same accusation restated until it hardens into a biography. Ninety-three minutes leaves no room for the long view, which suits the material — the film moves at the speed of a sentence being carried out. The National Board of Review placed it among the ten best of its year. What lingers is the plainness of the cause: one night's work by a man who did not ask who was knocking at his door.

Two hundred miles is what the new pass saves, and the whole film hangs off that number. A surveyor finds the route and is killed for it, leaving his son with both the survey and the grudge — the killer known by a right hand that has only two fingers on it. John Ford had 149 silent minutes in 1924 and spent them on scale: track gangs, weather, the slow work of laying rail across country that resists it, with a romance threaded through to keep the enterprise at human size. Two clocks run at once, the private and the national, and the private one keeps worse time. The National Film Registry holds a copy, which matters chiefly because a picture built this wide asks to be seen wide, on something larger than a desk.

A cat is handed from one girl to another, and the friendship works about the same way. Five schoolfriends in Korea have finished school; one has left for Seoul and an office; the others stay behind, and a group that used to be a fact becomes an arrangement requiring effort. Jeong Jae-eun takes 112 minutes to show what actually erodes a teenage alliance: train fares, shift work, the difference between a job and no job, the way one person's new vocabulary starts to embarrass everybody else. Nothing is announced. The drift arrives first as a scheduling difficulty, then as a habit, and the film trusts a viewer to notice it before the four of them do. The cat, meanwhile, keeps needing somewhere to sleep, which is the one obligation any of them can still meet.

A man plays a violin into a horn while two other men dance together. The violinist is William K.L. Dickson, who made the film; the horn belongs to a phonograph doing the half of the job that had not been done alongside pictures before, holding sound on wax while the camera held movement on film. About a minute survives, and it is the oldest sound film in which the two were recorded together. The dancing pair keep it from being only an engineering test — arms up, turning in a tight circle in a room built for experiments, with no audience but the equipment. The National Film Registry has it. A minute is not long enough to be a movie; it is long enough to be a room in 1894 that cannot now be unheard.

Over eleven hundred American soldiers were killed taking one small Italian village, and the film about it runs thirty-eight minutes. That ratio was John Huston's problem in 1945: how to account for a cost that size in a form that short, in a picture made by the army about the army that paid it. San Pietro was not a prize in itself. It stood in the road, and the road was the point, which is reasoning that looks clean on a map and looks different at ground level. A documentary produced this close to the event carries its own limits — what a camera can reach, what it is permitted to show, which of the dead can appear — and those limits are half of what a viewer now watches. The Academy Film Archive preserved it in 2005, so the grain and the sound still arrive as evidence rather than as damage.

The heel in professional wrestling is a job with duties: cheat where the crowd can see it, take the fall, make the other man look strong. Dae-ho, a bank clerk who is bullied at the office and produces nothing at his desk, takes that job in secret, and Kim Jee-woon spends 112 minutes on the gap between his two employments — one that requires him to absorb humiliation, one that pays him to perform it. The comedy is physical and deliberately unglamorous, a soft body learning how to fall. The mask is not a metaphor the film hurries to explain; it is a costume with rules, and rules turn out to be more use to Dae-ho than courage is. Then the second job stops staying inside its allotted hours, and the other half of the picture begins.

The subject is not the dancer but the cloth. Annabelle Moore, brought over from Broadway, holds a long diaphanous skirt out at arm's length and travels right and left across a bare stage while the fabric does the performing; William Heise's camera, in 1895, is there to establish whether a machine can hold that. Many prints went out hand-tinted, so the white cloth ran through colour as it turned — somebody at the very beginning of the medium decided the black-and-white record was insufficient and paid people to paint it, frame by frame, by hand. That labour is the interesting part. The dance was hers; the experiment was his. There is no story, no cut, no camera move: a stage, a body, and yards of moving material, about a minute of it, kept now by the National Film Registry.

Two high-school sophomores work out that they cost more at home than they are worth there, and leave. Tommy's mother has been out of work for months when Eddie's father loses his job; the boys head for the freight yards to look for the employment their parents could not find. William A. Wellman gets it done in sixty-eight minutes and allows no consolation on the way. What the film grasps is that a boxcar of runaway children is a society — with an economy, a hierarchy, and a standing quarrel with whoever owns the train — and that the country rolling past outside has already made up its mind about them. Made in 1933 about 1933, it has the unsettling quality of a report filed the same week as the events inside it.

The rule is arithmetic and it never bends: each image covers a tenth of the area of the one before. Charles Eames begins at the widest view anyone in 1977 could claim to have of the universe and works inward through every intervening scale to two people eating lunch in a park, then keeps going, through a man's hand and into the particles beneath the skin. Phil Morrison reads the figures. Nine minutes in total, and the discipline is the achievement: no dramatisation, no argument, only the same operation performed again and again until the middle of the range starts to look like the least explicable place on the ladder. The picnic is the one stop on the trip where anything is happening on a human timescale, and it is given no more screen time than a galaxy.

The room is shaped wrong, and that is the first honest thing in the film: an L, at the top of a cheap London boarding house, taken by a young Frenchwoman who is pregnant, unmarried, and not planning to resolve either condition in the usual ways. Jane's decision is made before the story starts; what follows is 126 minutes of consequence, played out on one staircase among tenants who ask fewer questions than the world downstairs would. Bryan Forbes lets the house stay a house — thin walls, shared landings, rent due on a fixed day — instead of promoting it to a symbol, and the affair Jane begins with a fellow boarder has to survive those acoustics. It took the BAFTA for Best British Film, though the real work in it is smaller than a prize: a woman counting weeks.

Two teenagers in 1940s New York decide to be friends, and the trouble is entirely with their fathers. Both families are Jewish and that is where the agreement ends: what a son should read, which language an argument belongs in, how much of the American century to admit through the front door. Jeremy Kagan keeps it to 107 minutes and mostly to interiors, because the picture is built on talk — study, dispute, the particular intimacy of two boys who can argue at that level and have nobody else to do it with. The decade supplies the pressure from outside; the rest comes from inside two households that would each prefer the other did not exist. It made the National Board of Review's ten best that year. The subject is inheritance, and how much of a father a son is permitted to keep.

The maidservant quits and walks out of the house, and everything follows from that door closing. A woman alone in the country with a baby, a tramp who notices she is alone, a husband too far off to help who steals a car to shorten the distance: eleven minutes, 1913, three places a viewer has to hold in mind at the same time. That is a problem of scheduling before it is a problem of fear, and Phillips Smalley solves it with cutting rate, sightlines and the geometry of a doorway. Nothing is supernatural and nothing is explained. The National Film Registry holds those eleven minutes; the tension in them is built out of distance and timing, and it still works on a viewer who can see exactly how the machine is assembled.

Jonathan Balser has views about his wife's clothes, her cooking and her friends, and he shares them in front of the children. Tina absorbs it, because absorbing it is the arrangement: a New York apartment, a household to run, a husband climbing socially at a rate that requires a wife who never embarrasses him. The affair she begins, with a writer whose cruelty at least comes in a more entertaining register, is not an escape and the film knows it — a lateral move between two men who both need an audience. Frank Perry plays a good deal of this as comedy, which is what makes it uncomfortable: the jokes land on a woman doing precisely what she was raised to want. The National Board of Review counted it among the year's ten best. Ninety-five minutes, 1970, and nobody in it apologises for anything.
